analysis.one_liner: Makes taxpayers whole when presidential business travel runs up government security and travel costs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote in the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone with Secret Service protection who travels to promote or benefit a business the President owns or profits from to pay the government back for the costs of that travel, including the cost of the security detail. Its target was the situation where presidential or related travel generates revenue for the President's private businesses while taxpayers cover the security bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently absorb the cost of Secret Service protection and other government expenses when presidential travel promotes the President's own businesses; they would be reimbursed by the protected traveler.

how_it_helps.text: Anyone receiving Secret Service protection who travels to promote or benefit a business the President owns or profits from must pay the government back for the travel's costs, including security.
It applies to travel by the President or other protectees, so taxpayers are not left covering security for trips that double as business promotion.

analysis.who_pays: Presidents with business interests, and anyone under their protection whose travel promotes those businesses, who would have to reimburse the Treasury for security and travel costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires reimbursement from the protected traveler, not directly from the President's business itself, so its practical force depends on how 'traveling in furtherance of' business interests is interpreted and enforced.

The bill only covers travel in furtherance of a business entity owned or controlled by the President or paying him; it would not reach other ways a sitting president could personally profit from office outside of business-related travel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending a practice where taxpayer-funded security bills pile up around travel that generates revenue for the President's businesses—is real but limited to presidents who own businesses, and its cost is essentially zero to the public. The drawback is modest: routing reimbursements through protectees rather than the President himself may leave some ambiguity, and operational costs of tracking business-related travel could add administrative burden. On balance a low-cost anti-self-dealing measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Oversight and Judiciary Committees and a Judiciary subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a vote, or a floor debate before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced November 15, 2019, the bill was referred to the House Oversight and Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
On December 18, 2019 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it stayed.
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill never received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Presidential business interests are better off; the requirement to repay security and travel costs never became law, and taxpayers continue to absorb those costs.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats; no Republican supported it, and it never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: Presidential businesses would lose the implicit subsidy of government-paid security and travel costs attached to visits promoting their properties. Ordinary taxpayers currently bear those costs.
The Treasury would be reimbursed for costs it currently absorbs when protectees travel for the President's business benefit.
